transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I came in because... I've been having these nights where I just eat and eat. And afterwards, I just sit there with crumbs and empty containers all around me, feeling so ashamed and... just disgusted with myself. It's gotten so bad that I can hardly even bring myself to pray, or look folks at church in the eye the next morning. I just knew I needed to talk to somebody.

After these eating episodes, do you do anything to try to get rid of the food or prevent weight gain—like making yourself throw up, using laxatives, exercising excessively, or restricting what you eat the next day?

No, I don't do any of that. I don't make myself sick or take anything like laxatives. I don't really exercise much either. I just... I just sit there with it, feeling awful about what I've done. I don't try to undo it, if that's what you mean.
How often do these eating episodes happen—like how many times per week would you say?

Well, since my friend passed away, it's been pretty frequent. I'd say these late-night eating spells happen at least once or twice most weeks. And, honestly, there hasn't been a single month where they really let up. It's just been a constant struggle.
During these eating episodes, do you feel like you're unable to stop eating, or do you feel like you could stop if you wanted to?

I definitely feel like I can't stop. It's... well, once I take that first bite after the house gets quiet, it's like my good sense just steps aside. Even while I'm sitting there telling myself, 'Belinda, stop now,' my hands just keep right on reaching for more. I want to stop, I really do, but I just can't seem to make myself do it.

During these eating episodes, would you say you're eating a much larger amount of food than most people would eat in a similar situation, or is it more of a normal amount that just feels out of control?

It's definitely a much larger amount than what anyone would normally eat. On a bad night... well, I can start with just a plate of leftover funeral-luncheon casserole. But before I know it, I've eaten that, plus half a pan of brownies, some biscuits, and whatever chicken salad is sitting in the fridge. Just all of it, right in one sitting.

During these eating episodes, do you feel like you're in a different mental state—like you're kind of detached or not fully aware of what you're doing—or are you fully aware the whole time that you're eating?
I'm fully aware of what I'm doing. I'm not... detached or anything like that. I know exactly what I'm eating and that I shouldn't be doing it, I just can't seem to stop myself.

When you're having these eating episodes, do you feel like you're eating an amount that's larger than what your body actually needs, or does it feel more like you're eating a normal amount but just can't control when to stop?

Well, like I was saying a minute ago, it's definitely way more than my body actually needs. I mean... nobody needs to eat a whole plate of casserole and half a pan of brownies just sitting there. It's far from a normal amount.
Have you noticed changes in your weight over the time you've been having these eating episodes? Has your weight gone up, or has it stayed about the same?
Well, my weight has actually stayed about the same. I haven't really noticed it going up or down, honestly.
On the days when you're not having these eating episodes, do you find yourself being very strict about what you eat, or do you try to eat very little to make up for the binge nights?
No, I don't really do that. I mean, I don't try to starve myself or go on any strict diets to make up for it. On the days I'm not having those episodes, I just eat my regular meals, like normal.

You mentioned you don't make yourself throw up or use laxatives. But I want to make sure I have the full picture—after these eating episodes, do you ever do anything else to try to burn off calories or compensate, like going for long walks, doing intense workouts, or eating very little the next day to make up for it?

No, I don't do any of that. I'm 65, so intense workouts aren't really my thing anyway. And like I said, I don't eat less the next day or anything. I just... I just feel awful about it, but I don't do anything to try and burn it off or make up for it.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient meets criteria for Binge Eating Disorder (F50.81). She reports recurrent binge eating episodes (at least 1-2 times per week for months since friend's death) characterized by: (1) consumption of objectively large quantities of food (casserole, half pan of brownies, biscuits, chicken salad in one sitting), (2) loss of control during episodes (unable to stop despite wanting to), and (3) marked distress and shame afterward. Critically, she denies compensatory behaviors (no purging, laxative use, excessive exercise, or restrictive eating), which distinguishes BED from Bulimia Nervosa. Weight has remained stable. Functional impairment is evident (shame affecting social/religious participation). Onset appears linked to psychosocial stressor (friend's death).
